background.definition: The focus of this review is on the midshaft and distal femur, patella, tibia, and fibula. Fractures of the proximal femur/hip and ankle are covered in separate chapters.

list.listitem: Femoral shaft fracture: most frequent in men after high-energy trauma and elderly women after low-energy fall.

Supracondylar/intracondylar femur fracture: high incidence in young adults from high-impact trauma and from elderly secondary to minor falls; distal femur fractures encompass 7% to 10% of all femur fractures.

Patellar fractures: 1% of all skeletal injuries; 2:1 male to female ratio; most common in individuals 20 to 50 years of age; bipartite patella, a fracture mimic, is present in 8% of the population (bilateral in 50%).

Tibial spine (eminence) fracture: Most common in children and adolescents; an ACL equivalent injury in children due to avulsion of incomplete ossification of the eminence; in adults, commonly due to high energy mechanism associated with concomitant injuries.
Tibial plateau fracture: 1% of all fractures; highest frequency between the 40-60 years old; 55-70% are isolated to the lateral plateau.
Tibial shaft fracture: most common long bone fracture; 26 fractures per 100,000 people years.
Fibula shaft fracture: uncommon isolated long bone fracture.
Blunt trauma
Motor vehicle trauma
Falls
Spontaneous or low-impact fracture in patients with osteoporosis, malignancy, or other pathology

Bisphosphonate use is associated with atypical hip and femoral shaft fractures. An atypical fracture may occur in 1 of every 278 women using bisphosphonates for over 5 years.This risk is higher with longer duration of bisphosphonate use and for Asian women.
Use Ottawa Knee Rules and Pittsburgh Knee Rules to decide whether radiographs are needed for knee injury. A
For all other parts of the leg consider radiographic imaging if there is significant bony tenderness, deformity on exam, and/or a concerning history for fracture. C
If there is a high clinical suspicion for compartment syndrome, compartment pressures should be obtained.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Classic features (pain, pallor, pulseless, paresthesias) poorly predictive; pain is the most sensitive and earliest finding; perfusion pressure <30 (DBP-compartment pressure) should be used for diagnosis.
Tenderness isolated to palpation of muscle without bony deformity or pain.
Instability of joint without bony tenderness; in the knee, multiligamentous rupture (3 of 4) is concerning for occult dislocation.
Deformity at joint space with inability to achieve full range of motion of the joint, pain with movement, and tenderness with palpation.
Joint line tenderness; can be associated with joint effusion acutely; sensation of knee popping, clicking, or locking.
Palpable defect with tenderness and swelling at site of rupture.
Overuse injury without history of trauma.
Young active patient with anterior knee pain worse with climbing stairs.
Pain over the anterolateral or posteromedial tibia; worse with activity.
Gradual onset of pain; history of diabetes, sickle cell, and/or chronic wounds are risk factors.
Inability to bear weight; joint effusion; secondary to bacteremia, direct inoculation via trauma or surgery, or contiguous spread (adjacent osteomyelitis).
Referred pain to thigh or knee; please see separate chapter for discussion.

list.listitem: Always assess distal neurovascular status. Obtain careful history of timing and mechanism of injury.
Femur fracture: palpate to assess for bone tenderness or deformity.
Knee fracture: both the Ottawa Knee Rulesand the Pittsburgh Knee Rules are useful in assessing which patients require knee imaging.
Tibia/fibula fracture: palpate to assess for bone tenderness or deformity.

The absence of pain, paresthesias, pain with passive stretch, and paresis decreases the likelihood of compartment syndrome, but if there is still a high-clinical suspicion, compartment pressures should be obtained.
Individuals with a recent increase in training intensity are at risk for stress fractures.

A proximal fibula fracture should prompt evaluation for concomitant deltoid ligament, medial malleolus, and/or syndesmotic injuries (also known as a Maisonneuve fracture). Assessment for peroneal nerve injury should be completed for proximal fibula fractures.
An occult fracture should be suspected if a patient has severe tenderness and difficulty with weight bearing after negative radiographs.
Use Pittsburgh Knee Rules and Ottawa Knees Rules to assess the need for X-rays.
For other parts of the leg, rely on the history and physical exam to determine which bones require X-ray imaging.

If suspicion for fracture is high and the X-ray appears normal, consider further evaluation with CT or MRI. CT is generally better in demonstrating anatomy of fracture and subluxations, whereas MRI is more useful to detect nondisplaced fractures, stress fractures, and ligamentous injuries.

For suspected tibial plateau fractures, AP, lateral, and oblique radiographs should be obtained. A 10 degree caudally tilted view can also be obtained to view for plateau articular stepoffs (as the plateau slopes anterior to posterior).
The lateral plateau is normally higher than the medial. If the lateral subchondral line is lower than the medial, assume a depressed fracture
A sunrise view should be obtained to fully evaluate for patella fractures.
If there is clinical suspicion for compartment syndrome, check compartment pressures.
When a fracture is thought to be secondary to child abuse, check a skeletal survey to look for evidence of other fractures.
Ultrasound examination is highly accurate for detecting long bone fractures of the leg.

Ottawa Knees Rules are effective at ruling out knee fracture; this is a helpful rule in determining appropriate use of radiography in evaluation of acute knee injuries. Furthermore, using the Ottawa Knee Rules to guide clinical practice decreases number of X-rays ordered, time spent in the ED, and cost of care.

Both the Ottawa Knee Rules and the Pittsburgh Knee Rules are sensitive and thus good at ruling out fractures, but the Pittsburgh Knee Rules have a higher specificity, making over-ordering of X-rays less likely.
Predictions for mortality and morbidity after orthopedic surgery can be analyzed using the POSSUM scoring system.
Evaluation of ankle injuries is further covered in the section on ankle injuries.
For all suspected fractures, assess for bony tenderness or deformity. If history and exam suggest a possible fracture, obtain an X-ray.
Use the Ottawa Knee Rule to determine need for radiographs.In cases of blunt trauma or fall, one can use the Pittsburgh Knee Rules.
Consider CT or MRI in cases of patellar fracture when it is difficult to discern whether the fracture is intra-articular.
Individuals with femoral shaft fractures can develop hemorrhagic shock secondary to third-space bleeding into the thigh, which can hold approximately 1/3 of a patient’s circulating blood volume.
Individuals can also develop fat embolism syndrome, which typically presents with hypoxemia, neurologic abnormalities, and a petechial rash
Consider CT or MRI imaging if radiographs are negative but there is high suspicion of fracture.
See for treatment recommendations.
For closed, well-aligned fractures, splinting and casting can be appropriate treatment. C
Intra-articular and open fractures necessitate emergent orthopedic evaluation and possible operative repair. C
Administer antibiotics when there is evidence of an open fracture. A

A systematic review concluded that, although there is some variability in studies, antibiotics reduce the incidence of early infections in open limb fractures. Both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms should be considered when opting for empirical treatment in open fractures.

Antibiotic choice for open fractures classically uses the Gustilo classification (). Gustilo Type I and II fractures are treated with a first generation cephalosporin (clindamycin for beta lactam allergic).

In Gustilo Type 3 fractures, broader gram-negative coverage is needed. This can be obtained by the addition of an aminoglycoside (gentamycin). Equally efficacious alternatives are ceftriaxone and piperacillin/tazobactam.
For wounds with potential fecal or clostridial contamination (such as farm-related injuries), high-dose penicillin should be added.

For delayed unions and nonunions, orthobiologics are becoming a more commonly utilized modality.This includes items such as mesenchymal stem cells, platelet-rich plasma, as well as various growth factors and hormones. Growth hormone has been shown to speed healing in closed tibial fractures.

A study identified 980 patients with tibial plateau or pilon fracture judged to be at high risk of infection, and randomized them to applicatin of intrawound vancomycin powder or usual care. The vancomycin group had a lower risk of deep infection (6.4% vs 9.8%, p = 0.06), primarily due to fewer gram positive infections (risk difference -3.7%, 95% CI -6.7% to -0.8%, NNT = 27).
Follow ACCP guidelines for anticoagulation to prevent venous thromboembolism.
Aspirin is non-inferior to enoxaparin to prevent venous thromboembolism for patients hospitalized with an acute fracure.

A large observational study found an association of bisphosphonate use following osteoporotic fracture with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.52-0.67). It may in part be explained by generally better health outcomes in patients who agree to take medications.
Please see for emergent and definitive therapy as indicated for each specific type of lower extremity fracture as well as recommendations on when to obtain an orthopedic consultation.

Skeletal pins located in areas with significant amount of soft tissue are at high risk for infection and pin site care with chlorhexidine 2 mg/mL solution is recommended based on expert opinion. However, multiple systematic reviews found insufficient evidence and no concensus for a cleaning protocol. Surgical technique for pin placement and implementation of a pin-site care protocol are the most important factors in reducing pin-site infections.

For 260 patients with severe open tibial shaft fracture randomized to internal fixation or modern external ring fixation, there was a greater risk of at least 1 major complication with external fixation (62% vs 43.7%, p = 0.005, NNTH = 5). The most important driver was a greater risk of reduction/implant failure with external fixation. There was no difference in the risk of infection.
A systematic review strongly supported occupational therapy and multidisciplinary rehabilitation for a variety of individuals with lower extremity musculoskeletal disorders.
Nonoperative treatment frequently involves splinting and casting.

A Cochrane review reported that current evidence is insufficient to routinely use low-intensity pulsed ultrasound, high-intensity focused ultrasound, and extracorporeal shockwave therapy for acute fractures.
Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound treatment should be considered for treatment of postoperative delayed union or nonunion of long bone fractures.
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy should also be considered as an effective treatment for non-union fractures with as comparable healing rates as surgical procedures.
Evidence does not support or refute hyperbaric oxygen therapy for promoting fracture healing and for treating nonunion; clinical trials are lacking.
Please see for appropriate referral and emergent consultation recommendations for each specific type of lower extremity fracture.
Prognosis depends on the severity and location of the fracture, as well as the health of the patient. C
Well-aligned, extra-articular fractures have a much better prognosis. C
Comminuted and intraarticular fractures often require operative repair and have much higher complication rates and a worse prognosis. C

feature.caption: Treatment of Lower Extremity Fracture.
feature.feature_body:
Fractures Emergent Treatment Definitive Treatment Additional Info
Femoral shaft fracture Middle Distal
Evaluate for other injuries;An association exists between femoral shaft fractures and ipsilateral femoral neck fractures and the diagnosis is often missed and treatment delayed Obtain emergent orthopedic consult Surgical treatment warranted unless patient is a poor surgical candidate; surgical options include intramedullary nailing, external fixation, and plating Patients are at risk for malalignment (midshaft fractures 2%, distal third 10%, proximal third 30%), delayed unions and nonunions, as well as pain and functional disability
Supracondylar/intracondylar femur fracture Extraarticular
Immobilize leg; consider orthopedic consult to arrange for prompt followup Nonsurgical treatment is an option if fracture is nondisplaced or if patient is nonambulatory; immobilize with long leg cast or brace
Supracondylar/intracondylar femur fracture Intraarticular
Emergent orthopedic consult Surgical fixation with plate or intramedullary nailing
Patellar fracture Nondisplaced/minimally displaced
Consider orthopedic consult to arrange for prompt followup Nonsurgical treatment if extensor mechanism is intact and less than 1-2 mm of step-off; full weight bearing in long leg cylinder cast or locked knee brace per orthopedics Knee immobilizer typically 4-6 weeks, early weight-bearing
Patellar fracture Displaced
Immobilize knee and obtain urgent orthopedic consult Surgical fixation with tension bands, screws, and/or wire; severely comminuted fracture may require partial patellectomy; occasional need for patellar tendon advancement Patients remain in a hinged knee brace for 6 weeks after surgery; complications include loss of fixation, delayed union, malunion, refracture, arthritis, and extensor lag
Tibial spine fracture (intracondylar aspect of tibial plateau; ACL insertion site) Nondisplaced
Immobilize leg in extension; consider orthopedic consult to arrange for prompt followup Partially displaced or hinged fractures can be managed nonoperatively
Tibial spine fracture Displaced
Immobilize leg and obtain urgent orthopedic consult Surgical intervention advised for displaced and comminuted fractures because of associated ACL incompetence; often open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) needed Postoperative active-assisted range of motion in a hinged brace encouraged with weight bearing in extension
Tibial plateau fracture Stable/extraarticular
Immobilize leg; consider orthopedic consult to arrange for prompt followup Nonsurgical treatment for stable, low-energy fractures and in nonambulatory patient; treat with immobilization and a hinged knee brace Weekly radiographs are obtained to ensure healing.Non-weight bearing until callus formation on radiographs, then progress to partial weight-bearing
Tibial plateau fracture Unstable/articular displacement
Immobilize leg and obtain urgent orthopedic consult Surgical treatment warranted in cases of unstable joint and articular displacement; options include ORIF and arthroscopic reduction and fixation Postoperative hinged brace is worn with delayed weight bearing Medial plateau fractures require more force than lateral plateau fractures and thus are often more obvious on radiographs.
Tibial shaft fracture Nondisplaced
Immobilize leg; consider orthopedic consult to arrange for prompt followup Closed treatment acceptable with <1 cm of shortening, <5 degrees of angulation in any plane, <5 degrees of rotational deformity after immobilization; proximal and distal shaft fractures are difficult to immobilize Risk for compartment syndrome
Tibial shaft fracture Displaced
Immobilize leg and obtain urgent orthopedic consult Surgical treatment is warranted; options include plate fixation, external fixation, and intramedullary nailing Risk for compartment syndromeHigher incidence of nonunion in cases of open fracture, fracture gap after fixation, and transverse fracture patterns
Fibula shaft fracture Nondisplaced
Immobilize leg; consider orthopedic consult to arrange for prompt followup Fracture reduction and long leg cast can be used for isolated, closed, minimally displaced fractures Union rates are as high as 97% Weight-bearing at tolerated, walking boot as needed for comfort
Fibula shaft fracture Displaced
Immobilize leg and obtain urgent orthopedic consult Surgical intervention should be considered including IM nailing, external fixation, and/or plates and screws Complications include malunion, nonunion, and hardware breakage
Data modified from Ricci WM. Femur: trauma. Vaccaro AR, ed. Orthopaedic Knowledge Update 8, Vol 2. Rosemont, IL: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. 2005;33:425–431.
